mission: Aftermath of Iressa's death. Talon presses Ben about the option he refused. Ben cannot cleanly answer whether it would have worked. While they process the loss, they examine Iressa's dying transmission and find what she actually sent: a documentary reconstruction tying the Foundation, Korda, and the Iresh thread together — and the strategic revelation about the holocron's identity-shaping purpose, with Jacen's own annotation making the intent unmistakable. This is the case Saba would need — if there were time to bring it.
why_now: Iressa’s death and the transmission she sent have changed the shape of what Ben is carrying. The documentary chain now exists — enough to go to Saba. But the Vigil is already moving on Iresh, and institutional review takes weeks Ben doesn’t have. This is the moment he has to decide whether to wait for the Order to ratify his findings or start building what he needs to move himself.
conflict: Ben owes Talon an honest answer about the coercive option he refused and does not have one. The transmission demands attention neither of them can give cleanly through grief — and what it reveals is larger and worse than the case they thought they were building.
turning_point: Iressa's transmission reveals what the holocron is for — identity-level influence — under Jacen's own annotation.
closing_hook: Jacen's annotation sits on the screen between them: the holocron was built to shape who people are. Iressa died sending them proof.
setting: Coruscant, Iressa's secondary cache — a quiet leased basement workshop in the warehouse district she had maintained for years, separate from Civitas and from her residence. Old terminals, hand-labelled crates of datachips, the smell of soldering paste. Ben and Talon work here for several days after the archive disaster. Two short holocalls (Luke first, then Saba) happen from this room.
emotional_trajectory: Iressa’s death proves restraint can cost lives. The Midpoint should land as both emotional cost and strategic clarity. Ben’s decision should feel like the moment he stops being a victim of the past and starts acting on it — even when the method carries danger. The two holo calls (Luke, Saba) should establish that Ben tried the right way first. The institutional path is not refused out of arrogance; it is refused after being tried. Saba is not the villain. The slowness is. Reader-onboarding / clarity note: Plain-language consequence: Iressa died protecting the clue. The clue tells them the enemy is already on Iresh and tells them why it matters (identity-shaping). The Order will review the case properly, which means weeks Ben does not have. He chooses to keep building evidence and prepare to move on Iresh himself. Continuity / craft notes: - This is Pinch Point 1’s emotional aftermath and the Midpoint structural pivot, in the same chapter. - The drafter should not let the holo calls become exposition. They are short. Luke’s call is paternal; Saba’s call is institutional. Both end with Ben understanding the cost of doing things the right way. - Ben’s decision should be quiet, not declamatory. He does not announce it. He simply starts working on what comes next. Talon notices and follows.

stakes.personal: The Midpoint is the moment Ben stops being a victim of the past and starts acting on it. His decision to move outside official channels is quiet, not declamatory — but it is the moment his self-definition engine shifts. He is not waiting for the Order to tell him what his past means. He is going to use it.
stakes.interpersonal: Talon presses Ben about the option he refused in the archive. Ben can't cleanly answer whether it would have worked. This is the first honest conversation between them about what Jacen actually taught Ben — not the category of it, but the specific usable version that Ben carries. Talon doesn't simplify it. Neither does Ben.
stakes.external: Iressa's dying transmission contains two things: the documentary chain needed to bring Saba a case, and the strategic revelation — Jacen's unfinished holocron systematizes Recognition and Holding for identity-level influence, and Iressa found Jacen's own sealed annotation naming the cache's purpose. The Vigil intends to use Aevyn, as Jacen's surviving student, to complete the work on Iresh. The institutional path is too slow. The documentary case is at Iressa's secondary cache. Moving to Iresh has to start now.

sensory_details: Iressa's secondary cache smells of soldering paste and old datachip cases — a workspace, not a home. The holo projector for the Luke call is small and set on a crate; Luke's face in the projection looks tired in a way Ben doesn't quite remember, his eyes slightly further away even when he's looking right at Ben. The Saba call is colder — Barabel gravity through a mid-grade encrypting chip, no warmth in the static.
canon_elements_needed: Shedu Maad / Hapes Jedi HQ continuity
Iresh physical geography and local survival rules

turning_point_detail.trigger: The dying transmission decrypts into two layers: the documentary chain, and the strategic revelation about Recognition and Holding as an identity-influence tool — annotated in Jacen's own hand.
turning_point_detail.shift: The case stops being about a hidden shipment and becomes about what the shipment protects. The Vigil isn't recovering history; it is reaching for a tool that shapes people.
turning_point_detail.cost: Iressa's death was the price of this knowledge, and Ben cannot answer Talon's question about whether his restraint helped kill her.

emotional_arc.start: Grief and guilt over Iressa — Talon's direct question about the refused option cuts through. Ben can't give a clean answer.
emotional_arc.shift: The transmission turns mourning into obligation: what Iressa sent is bigger than either of them expected, and it is addressed, deliberately, to them.
emotional_arc.end: Ben and Talon sit with the size of it. The documentary chain exists. The question now is who can act on it in time — and both of them are afraid they already know the answer.

key_beats.beat_description: Talon presses Ben directly about the option he refused; Ben cannot give a clean answer about whether it would have worked.
key_beats.state_change: The first honest exchange about what Jacen actually taught Ben — not the category, the specific usable technique.
key_beats.pov_reaction: The pause before answering that is itself an answer — the absence of a ready line, which is the most honest thing he has said in days.

key_beats.beat_description: Ben and Talon examine Iressa's dying transmission: the documentary reconstruction and the strategic revelation about Recognition and Holding as an identity-influence tool, with Jacen's own annotation.
key_beats.state_change: The threat is now named and evidenced — not a theory about Jacen's legacy but a specific operational intent with a specific human carrier.
key_beats.pov_reaction: Reading Jacen's own annotation and the still quality that comes when something confirms what you feared but could not prove.

key_beats.beat_description: Jacen's annotation in the reconstruction's margin makes the purpose unmistakable — this is not archive housekeeping; this is the documented intent behind the holocron, in the hand of the man who built it.
key_beats.state_change: The evidence is now complete enough to take to Saba — the chain Iressa died to preserve is real, legible, and devastating.
key_beats.pov_reaction: the cold settling of confirmation — worse than suspicion because it removes the version of events where he was wrong
